title: The CT scanner

confidence.note: The first clinical scan is dated by the hospital and EMI records, and the 1979 Nobel citation and patent history fix the surrounding chronology. Only the popular story of who paid for it is in doubt.

people: Godfrey Hounsfield (1919–2004), EMI engineer who designed and built the scanner
James Ambrose, radiologist who ran the first clinical scans
Allan Cormack (1924–1998), Tufts physicist who worked out the reconstruction mathematics
summary: An engineer at a record company found a way to see inside the living skull. The first patient's scan took two days to compute.
body: On 1 October 1971, at Atkinson Morley's Hospital in Wimbledon, a middle-aged woman with a suspected tumor in her left frontal lobe became the first living patient examined by a scanner built by Godfrey Hounsfield, an engineer at the British firm EMI. The data had to be processed on an off-site mainframe computer, and the radiologist James Ambrose waited two days to see the pictures. They showed a cystic tumor, which surgeons then removed.

Hounsfield had the idea in 1967. Ordinary X-ray film flattens the body into overlapping shadows; his machine swept a beam through one slice from many directions and let a computer calculate the density of each small square. It was built on a shoestring, about £69,000 in three years, with seed money from the British Department of Health and Social Security. Unknown to him, the physicist Allan Cormack at Tufts University had worked out the underlying mathematics in papers of 1963 and 1964. By late 1973 scanners were running in Manchester, Glasgow, London and at the Mayo Clinic, and in 1979 Hounsfield and Cormack shared the Nobel Prize.

myth.tradition: The CT scanner was paid for by EMI's profits from Beatles records.
myth.record: EMI's music wealth may help explain why it could employ a free-thinking inventor, but the project was funded mostly by a grant from the British Department of Health and Social Security.

links.note: CT reassembles ordinary X-ray measurements into cross-sections.
MRI borrowed CT's idea of reconstructing slices by computer.
Another postwar way of seeing inside the body.

title: Psychiatry redraws its map

confidence.note: The 1973 decision, the referendum and DSM-III's 1980 publication are documented. How far Rosenhan's study shaped DSM-III is argued from interviews, and the study itself is now widely doubted.

people: David Rosenhan, psychologist, author of 'On Being Sane in Insane Places'
Robert Spitzer, psychiatrist who chaired the DSM-III task force
summary: In 1973 a famous experiment mocked psychiatric diagnosis and the profession voted that homosexuality was not an illness. A new rulebook followed.
body: In 1973 *Science* published David Rosenhan's 'On Being Sane in Insane Places', claiming that healthy volunteers who reported hearing voices were admitted to psychiatric hospitals and labeled schizophrenic. That December, after gay activists had disrupted the 1970 and 1971 meetings of the American Psychiatric Association, its trustees removed homosexuality from the diagnostic manual; 58% of 10,000 voting members upheld the decision. Robert Spitzer then chaired the task force for DSM-III (1980), which built diagnoses on explicit criteria rather than theory. Rosenhan's study has since been seriously questioned.

myth.tradition: Rosenhan's experiment proved that psychiatrists cannot tell the sane from the insane.
myth.record: Psychiatrists attacked its design from the start, and a 2019 investigation, *The Great Pretender*, argued it was exaggerated and possibly dishonest, though outright fraud cannot be proven.

links.note: DSM-III revived Kraepelin's descriptive approach to diagnosis.
Drugs and deinstitutionalization formed the backdrop to the 1970s crisis.

title: Magnetic resonance imaging

confidence.note: Lauterbur's paper is dated 16 March 1973 and the later milestones are published papers. Who deserves credit for inventing MRI is genuinely contested, as the 2003 Nobel dispute showed.

people: Paul Lauterbur (1929–2007), chemist who made the first magnetic resonance images
Peter Mansfield (1933–2017), Nottingham physicist who developed fast imaging
Raymond Damadian, physician who proposed NMR for detecting tumors
summary: Two tubes of water in a magnet produced the first magnetic resonance image. Who invented MRI is still argued over.
body: Hydrogen nuclei in a strong magnetic field absorb and re-emit radio waves at a frequency set by the field's strength. In a short *Nature* paper of March 1973, the chemist Paul Lauterbur showed that by adding gradients, so that the field varied across a sample, he could tell where each signal came from and build a picture. His first image distinguished tubes of ordinary water from heavy water. In Nottingham the physicist Peter Mansfield worked out how to analyze such signals quickly and showed that very fast imaging was possible.

Others got to the body first. In 1971 Raymond Damadian had reported in *Science* that tumors and normal tissue give different magnetic signals, and in 1977 he published an image of a human chest, the same year another group imaged a living wrist. Commercial scanners appeared in 1980. When the 2003 Nobel Prize went to Lauterbur and Mansfield alone, Damadian protested loudly and divided the field. The rivals had long ignored each other: neither cited the other's key paper.

myth.tradition: Raymond Damadian single-handedly invented MRI and was simply cheated of a Nobel Prize.
myth.record: Damadian first saw NMR's promise for detecting cancer and made an early human scan, but modern imaging rests on Lauterbur's gradients and Mansfield's methods. Credit was shared among several groups and remains disputed.

links.note: MRI images the body without ionizing radiation.

title: Recombinant DNA

confidence.note: The 1973 paper, the Asilomar meeting, the patent and the 1982 insulin approval are all documented. Historians debate whose contributions have been underplayed, not whether the events happened.

people: Herbert Boyer, UCSF biochemist and Genentech co-founder
Annie Chang and Robert Helling, co-authors of the 1973 paper
Paul Berg (1926–2023), Stanford biochemist and Asilomar organizer
summary: Two Californian scientists learned to cut and paste genes into bacteria. Within a decade, bacteria were making human insulin.
body: In 1973 Stanley Cohen of Stanford and Herbert Boyer of the University of California, San Francisco, with Annie Chang and Robert Helling, cut bacterial plasmids (small rings of DNA) with a restriction enzyme, joined fragments from different plasmids and put the result into *E. coli*. The new plasmids worked and were copied as the bacteria divided. Paul Berg's Stanford laboratory had already joined DNA from two unrelated species in 1971 but chose not to put it into bacteria. Cohen and Boyer's method made cloning genes routine.

The power alarmed biologists. After a voluntary pause, they met at Asilomar in California in February 1975 and agreed to go on under graded safety rules, which became the NIH guidelines. Commerce moved faster than regulation: Stanford filed a patent in November 1974, Boyer co-founded Genentech in 1976, and in 1978 Genentech scientists cloned a synthetic human insulin gene and signed with Eli Lilly. In 1982 recombinant human insulin became the first therapeutic protein made this way to be approved by the US Food and Drug Administration.

links.note: Gene splicing depended on understanding DNA's structure.
Bacterial human insulin replaced insulin extracted from animal pancreases.
Later hepatitis B vaccines were made by recombinant DNA.
Gene therapy uses the same cut-and-paste tools.

title: Monoclonal antibodies

confidence.note: The Nature paper of August 1975, the 1984 Nobel Prize and the 1986 approval of OKT3 are all documented.

place: Medical Research Council laboratory, Cambridge, England
summary: Fusing a cancer cell with an antibody-making cell produced an immortal factory for a single antibody. Nobody patented it.
body: In August 1975 Georges Köhler and César Milstein reported fusing antibody-making mouse spleen cells with cancerous myeloma cells. The hybrids, called hybridomas, grew indefinitely and each secreted one predefined antibody. Britain's patenting body saw no obvious commercial use. The first therapeutic monoclonal antibody, muromonab-CD3 (OKT3), was approved in 1986 to fight kidney-transplant rejection; by the mid-2020s more than 200 antibody drugs were in late-stage trials. Köhler and Milstein shared the 1984 Nobel Prize.

links.note: Antibody serum therapy began with diphtheria antitoxin.
Antibodies against amyloid are a recent use.
